# Introduction to graph theory {#sec-graphs}

Many biological systems are naturally described as networks: proteins that bind one another, genes that regulate one another, metabolites linked by reactions. Before building detailed dynamic models of such systems, a great deal can be learnt from the structure of the network alone. This chapter sets up the representation of networks in both languages; @sec-networks then measures their structure.

### Adjacency matrix

A network, or graph, is a set of nodes joined by edges. For an undirected network of $n$ nodes, the **adjacency matrix** $\mathbf{A}$ has $a_{ij} = 1$ if nodes $i$ and $j$ are joined, and 0 otherwise.

In MATLAB, networks are `graph` objects (or `digraph` for directed networks), part of core MATLAB. In Python, the standard package is NetworkX. Both provide shortest paths and centrality measures; we compute the clustering coefficient and closeness from their definitions, so that both languages use exactly the same formulas as the book.

| | MATLAB | Python (NetworkX) |
|---|---|---|
| Build a network | `G = graph(s, t)` | `G = nx.Graph(); G.add_edges_from(edges)` |
| Adjacency matrix | `adjacency(G)` (sparse) | `nx.to_numpy_array(G)` |
| Degrees | `degree(G)` | `dict(G.degree())` |
| Shortest-path lengths | `distances(G)` | `nx.floyd_warshall_numpy(G)` |
| Betweenness | `centrality(G, 'betweenness')` | `nx.betweenness_centrality(G, normalized=False)` |
